Study on the Expression of Human β-Defensin-3 in Sporotrichosis Lesions and Its Clinical Correlations
Study on the Expression of Human β-Defensin-3 in Sporotrichosis Lesions and Its Clinical Correlations

rightsList.rights: Creative Commons Attribution Non Commercial No Derivatives 4.0 International

descriptions.description: 1. Expression characteristics of hBD-3 in sporotrichosis lesions and its correlation with clinical characteristics: Compared with healthy controls, hBD-3 expression was significantly increased in sporotrichosis lesions (P < 0.0001), mainly localized to the spinous and basal layers of the epidermis. hBD-3 expression was higher in the early stage of disease duration (≤2 months; P = 0.0296), and was negatively correlated with disease duration within the first year (r = -0.2518, P = 0.0282). hBD-3 expression was higher in lesions from patients with the lymphocutaneous form than in those with the fixed cutaneous form (P = 0.0120). hBD-3 expression was also significantly negatively correlated with fungal burden in lesions (r = -0.6008, P < 0.0001).2. Correlation of hBD-3 expression with local and systemic inflammatory responses in sporotrichosis lesions: hBD-3 expression was significantly positively correlated with the area of dermal MPO+ neutrophil infiltration (r = 0.5922, P = 0.0011), but showed no significant correlation with the infiltration of CD4+ T cells (r = 0.1038, P = 0.6633), CD8+ T cells (r = -0.2722, P = 0.2457) or CD68+ macrophages (r = 0.1434, P = 0.5701). Among systemic inflammatory markers, local hBD-3 expression in lesions showed no correlation with plasma levels of CRP or most chemokines (all P > 0.05), and was negatively correlated only with plasma CXCL3 levels (r = -0.6214, P = 0.0155).3. Correlation of hBD-3 expression w clinical manifestations in sporotrichosis lesions: hBD-3 expression was significantly higher in lesions with ulceration or erosion than those without (P < 0.0001). Univariable logistic regression showed that the percentage of hBD-3 positive area was significantly associated with ulcer formation in lesions (OR = 1.249, 95% CI: 1.087–1.434, P = 0.0017). After adjustment for age, sex, disease duration, and clinical type, this association remained significant (adjusted OR = 1.278, 95% CI: 1.093–1.493, P = 0.0021).

titles.title: From lab to field: Mating-dependent gut enlargement and immune suppression in field-caught Aedes aegypti

descriptions.description: This dataset contains the raw data underlying all figures and supplementary figures in Girard-Mejia et al., including morphometric measurements of wing length and midgut diameter, relative gene expression values for antimicrobial peptide genes, Toll pathway regulators in midgut and carcass tissue, and kr-h1 in midgut , 16S rRNA bacterial abundance counts, and Zika virus infection prevalence data from pooled mosquito samples collected in Comapa, Jutiapa, Guatemala. Data were generated from field-caught adult Aedes aegypti females and laboratory-reared adults emerging from field-collected immature stages, comparing virgin and mated individuals across gravid and non-gravid physiological states.

titles.title: Surface Modification Techniques to Enhance Antibacterial Properties of Dental Polyetheretherketone (PEEK) Implants: A Systematic Review
Surface Modification Techniques to Enhance Antibacterial Properties of Dental Polyetheretherketone (PEEK) Implants: A Systematic Review

descriptions.description:
Polyetheretherketone (PEEK) is increasingly explored as a dental implant material due to its favorable mechanical properties and radiolucency. However, its bioinert and hydrophobic surface can lead to poor osseointegration and bacterial colonization. Various surface-modification techniques — including plasma treatments, chemical sulfonation, nanoparticle coatings, antimicrobial peptide functionalization, and incorporation of bioactive ceramics — have been developed to impart antibacterial activity while maintaining biocompatibility.

Despite growing literature, there is no consolidated systematic review summarizing the antibacterial efficacy of these surface modifications, particularly in dental applications. This review aims to synthesize current evidence and identify the most promising surface-engineering strategies for antibacterial enhancement of PEEK implants.
Purpose of the Study

The purpose of this systematic review is to identify, evaluate, and summarize current evidence on surface modification techniques used to enhance the antibacterial properties of dental PEEK implants. The review will aim to:

Classify and compare different surface modification techniques (physical, chemical, and coating-based).

Assess the antibacterial efficacy of these modifications using quantitative data (e.g., bacterial colony reduction, inhibition zones, biofilm inhibition percentages).

Evaluate the biocompatibility and cytotoxicity associated with these modifications to ensure clinical safety.

Expected Outcomes

The review is expected to yield:

A comprehensive classification of antibacterial surface-modification strategies applied to dental PEEK implants.

Quantitative and qualitative evidence on the most effective approaches for reducing bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation.

Identification of safe and biocompatible modifications with potential for clinical translation

titles.title: How far does a random forest generalize from a 54-run LAMMPS+SPICA benchmark?

descriptions.description: Selecting near-optimal hybrid MPI+OpenMP configurations for molecular dynamics workloads on modern HPC clusters has traditionally required exhaustive empirical benchmarking, consuming allocation budget proportional to the number of configurations evaluated. This work investigates whether a cold-start Random Forest surrogate, trained once on a small, structured benchmark dataset, can reliably predict execution performance and recommend high-performing configurations without further cluster runs. The training dataset comprises 54 LAMMPS+SPICA runs of the antimicrobial peptide Tritrpticin on a hydrated DOPC bilayer (4 354 coarse-grained beads), spanning 18 hybrid configurations on 1-8 AMD EPYC 7662 nodes of the Lovelace cluster at CENAPAD-SP, with three independent replications each. Nine topology and resource features feed five regressors that predict loop time and four internal LAMMPS timing fractions (Pair, Kspace, Comm, Modify). In-sample mean absolute error is 0.49 s on loop time (4.0 % relative). Feature importance localizes predictive signal in topology variables (OpenMP threads and MPI/OpenMP ratio dominate; raw node and core counts contribute under 3 %). Leave-one-dimension-out generalization reveals that accuracy is governed by hardware regime membership: within a common regime (single-node, multi-node, or shared threading tier) the surrogate ranks configurations correctly, and degrades when targets cross architectural boundaries. The result is an interpretable map of where the surrogate's recommendations can be trusted, useful for scoping further benchmark campaigns at a fraction of their nominal cost.

titles.title: Antimicrobial peptide PMAP-36 attenuates ExPEC-induced neuroinflammation by inhibiting the NF-κB/NLRP3 pathway through autophagy activation

descriptions.description: Supplementary materialsFigure S1. The biocompatible effect of PMAP-36 in vitro and in vivo. (A) The viability of BV2 cells treated with PMAP-36 (0.625 μM or 1.25 μM) for 12 h, followed by washing and then incubation for an additional 24 h, was detected via the CCK-8 assay. Mice (total N=36) were intraperitoneally injected with 5 mg/kg PMAP-36 or PBS as a negative control. (B) Body weight was monitored daily for 7 d, and variations in body weights (%) (total N=12, per group n=6) are shown. (C-F) Blood was collected to determine biochemical indicators, including alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (C), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (D), urea (UREA) (E) and inorganic phosphate (IP) (F). Different tissues (total N=6, per group n=3), including the brain, lung, liver, and spleen, were collected to observe histopathological changes. (G) Representative images of histopathological changes in tissues are shown. A is representative of three independent experiments with five samples. B-F are representative of two independent experiments with six mice. G is representative of two independent experiments with three samples. All data are presented as the means ± SEM. ns = not significant.Figure S2. The effect of PMAP-36 on bacterial invasion in BV2 cells. (A) The number of intracellular bacteria in ExPEC-infected BV2 cells with PMAP-36 treatment under the condition of 3-MA and CQ at 1 and 2 h post infection. Data are presented as the means ± SEM and representative of three independent experiments with triplicate samples. ***P ≤ 0.001, ns = not significant.Supplementary File 1. titles.title: PETAL (Pattern-Enforced Transformer for Antimicrobial peptide Learning)

descriptions.description:
PETAL (Pattern-Enforced Transformer for Antimicrobial peptide Learning) is a generative AI pipeline for de novo design of antimicrobial peptides against Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA persisters and biofilms. The pipeline integrates a GPT-style language model with dual random forest regressors to generate, score, and rank novel peptide candidates by predicted therapeutic index before synthesis and experimental testing.

The repository contains two components. PETAL-GPT is a causal transformer (~207,000 parameters) trained on 1,831 S. aureus-active peptide sequences from the Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP). It generates novel 12-mer candidates across nine configurations spanning three amino acid series (PETAL-N, PETAL-E, PETAL-A) and three net positive charge targets (+2, +3, +4) using a pattern-biased decoding strategy with adaptive relaxation. PETAL-TI trains two independent random forest regressors — one for antimicrobial potency (log₂ MIC against S. aureus, n = 3,779 sequences) and one for mammalian cell toxicity (log₂ CC50/HC50, n = 905 sequences) — and combines predictions into a therapeutic index score to rank candidates by predicted selectivity.

This release accompanies the manuscript: "PETAL: A Generative AI Framework for De Novo Design of Potent and Selective Antimicrobial Peptides Against MRSA Persisters and Biofilms." Houston Methodist Research Institute.
